questions.question: What is an array in C++?
options: A collection of elements of different data types
A collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory
questions.explanation: An array is a collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations.

questions.question: What is the correct way to declare a 1D array of 5 integers?
questions.explanation: The syntax for a 1D array is: data_type array_name[size];

questions.question: What is the index of the first element of an array?
questions.explanation: In C++, array indexing starts at 0.

questions.question: If an array has 10 elements, what is the valid index range?
questions.explanation: Valid indices are from 0 to size-1.

questions.question: How do you access the third element of an array arr?
questions.explanation: The third element is at index 2 (0-based indexing).

questions.question: What is the correct way to initialize an array with values?
questions.explanation: Arrays are initialized using braces with comma-separated values.

questions.question: What happens if you partially initialize an array?
questions.explanation: In C++, if you initialize fewer elements, the rest are automatically set to 0.

questions.question: What is a multidimensional array?
options: An array with more than one dimension
questions.explanation: A multidimensional array has more than one index, such as a 2D array.

questions.question: What is the correct declaration of a 2D array of 3 rows and 4 columns?
questions.explanation: The syntax is: data_type array_name[rows][columns];

questions.question: How do you access the element in the second row and third column of a 2D array?
questions.explanation: Indices are 0-based: second row is index 1, third column is index 2.

questions.question: How are elements of a 2D array stored in memory?
questions.explanation: C++ stores 2D arrays in row-major order.

questions.question: How do you pass a 1D array to a function?
questions.explanation: Arrays are passed as pointers, so int arr[] or int *arr is used.

questions.question: When you pass an array to a function, what is actually passed?
options: A copy of the entire array
The address of the first element
questions.explanation: Arrays decay to pointers, so the address of the first element is passed.

questions.question: Can you return an array from a function directly?
options: No, you must return a pointer or use a reference
questions.explanation: Arrays cannot be returned by value; you can return a pointer to a dynamically allocated array or use std::array/vector.

questions.question: What is an array of objects?
options: An array where each element is an object of a class
questions.explanation: An array of objects stores multiple objects of the same class.

questions.question: How do you create an array of 5 objects of class Student?
questions.explanation: The syntax is: ClassName arrayName[size];

questions.question: When an array of objects is created, which constructor is called?
questions.explanation: If no initializer is provided, the default constructor is called for each object.

questions.question: What is a string in C++?
questions.explanation: A string is a sequence of characters.

questions.question: Which header file is required to use std::string?
questions.explanation: The <string> header provides the std::string class.

questions.question: How do you declare a C-style string?
questions.explanation: A C-style string is an array of characters ending with a null character.

questions.question: What is the null character in a C-style string?
questions.explanation: C-style strings are terminated by the null character '\0'.

questions.question: How do you declare a string object in C++?
questions.explanation: std::string is the standard string class; you can also use string if using namespace std is declared.

questions.question: What is the difference between a string variable and a string constant?
options: String constant can be modified; string variable cannot
String variable can be modified; string constant cannot
questions.explanation: A string constant (e.g., const char*) is read-only, while a string variable can be changed.

questions.question: How do you find the length of a std::string?
questions.explanation: Both length() and size() return the number of characters in a std::string.

questions.question: How do you concatenate two std::string objects?
questions.explanation: The + operator concatenates two std::string objects.

questions.question: What is an array of strings?
options: An array where each element is a string
questions.explanation: An array of strings can be an array of std::string objects or a 2D char array.

questions.question: How do you declare an array of 3 std::string objects?
questions.explanation: You can use std::string arr[3]; or string arr[3]; if using namespace std.

questions.question: How do you declare a 2D character array to store 3 strings of max length 20?
questions.explanation: A 2D char array with rows for strings and columns for characters.

questions.question: Can a class have a string as a data member?
questions.explanation: A class can have std::string as a data member.

questions.question: What happens when you assign a string literal to a char array?
options: The array points to the string literal
The string is copied into the array with a null terminator
questions.explanation: char arr[] = "Hello"; copies the characters and adds '\0'.

questions.question: What is the output of: char str[] = "Hello"; cout << str[1];
questions.explanation: Index 1 corresponds to the second character, 'e'.

questions.question: What is the output of: std::string s = "Hello"; cout << s.size();
questions.explanation: The string "Hello" has 5 characters.

questions.question: How do you access the first character of a std::string?
questions.explanation: Indexing starts at 0, so s[0] is the first character.

questions.question: What is the correct way to compare two std::string objects?
questions.explanation: std::string supports == for comparison.

questions.question: What is the difference between char[] and std::string?
options: char[] is dynamic; std::string is fixed
char[] is a fixed-size array; std::string is a dynamic class
char[] is a class; std::string is an array
questions.explanation: char[] has fixed size and manual memory management; std::string manages memory automatically.

questions.question: What is the size of an empty std::string?
questions.explanation: An empty std::string has size 0.

questions.question: How do you read a string with spaces using cin?
questions.explanation: getline(cin, str) reads a whole line including spaces.

questions.question: What does the following code do? int arr[5] = {1,2};
options: Initializes first two elements to 1,2 and rest to 0
questions.explanation: Partial initialization fills the remaining elements with 0.

questions.question: What is the correct entry point of a C++ program?
questions.explanation: Execution of a C++ program begins from the main() function.

questions.question: What is the correct basic structure of a C++ program?
questions.explanation: A C++ program typically starts with #include directives, followed by the main() function containing statements.

questions.question: Which header file is required to use cout and cin?
questions.explanation: <iostream> is the standard header for input/output streams like cout and cin.

questions.question: What is the correct way to include a header file in C++?
questions.explanation: Preprocessor directives start with #, and #include is used to include header files.

questions.question: What does the #include directive do?
options: Includes the contents of another file before compilation
questions.explanation: #include is a preprocessor directive that inserts the contents of the specified file into the source code before compilation.

questions.question: Which preprocessor directive is used to define a constant or macro?
questions.explanation: #define is used to define macros or symbolic constants.

questions.question: Which symbol is used for a single-line comment in C++?
questions.explanation: // is used for single-line comments, while /* */ is used for multi-line comments.

questions.question: Which of the following is a multi-line comment in C++?
questions.explanation: /* ... */ is used for multi-line comments in C++.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using namespace std;?
options: To avoid writing std:: before standard library names
questions.explanation: using namespace std; allows you to use standard library names (like cout, cin) without prefixing them with std::.

questions.question: Which data type is used to store a single character?
questions.explanation: char stores a single character, e.g., 'A'.

questions.question: Which data type is used to store whole numbers?
questions.explanation: int is used to store integer (whole) numbers.

questions.question: Which data type is used to store decimal numbers with single precision?
questions.explanation: float stores single-precision floating-point (decimal) numbers.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a primitive data type in C++?
questions.explanation: string is a class in the standard library, not a primitive data type.

questions.question: What is the size of an int typically in C++?
questions.explanation: On most modern systems, int is 4 bytes, though it is platform-dependent.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid variable declaration?
questions.explanation: The correct syntax is: data_type variable_name; e.g., int x;

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid variable name?
questions.explanation: Variable names can start with an underscore or letter, but not with a digit or hyphen, and cannot be keywords.

questions.question: What is the default value of a local variable in C++?
questions.explanation: Local variables are not automatically initialized; they contain garbage values.

questions.question: What is implicit type conversion also known as?
questions.explanation: Implicit conversion is done automatically by the compiler.

questions.question: What is explicit type conversion also known as?
questions.explanation: Explicit conversion is also called type casting, where the programmer specifies the conversion.

questions.question: Which C++ operator is used for explicit type conversion?
questions.explanation: C++ provides static_cast, dynamic_cast, const_cast, and reinterpret_cast for explicit conversions.

questions.question: Which type conversion may cause data loss?
questions.explanation: Narrowing conversion (e.g., float to int) may lose data such as the fractional part.

questions.question: What is the result of 5 / 2 in C++ (integer division)?
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates the decimal part, so 5/2 gives 2.

questions.question: Which operator is used to find the remainder of division?
questions.explanation: % is the modulus operator, used to find the remainder.

questions.question: What is the output of 10 % 3?
questions.explanation: 10 divided by 3 gives remainder 1.

questions.question: What is the output of 5 + 3 * 2?
questions.explanation: Multiplication (*) has higher precedence than addition (+), so 3*2=6, then 5+6=11.

questions.question: What does a relational operator return?
questions.explanation: Relational operators return a boolean value: true or false.

questions.question: Which operator represents logical AND?
questions.explanation: && is the logical AND operator.

questions.question: Which operator represents logical OR?
questions.explanation: || is the logical OR operator.

questions.question: Which operator represents logical NOT?
questions.explanation: ! is the logical NOT operator.

questions.question: What is the output of (5 > 3) ? "Yes" : "No"?
questions.explanation: The condition 5 > 3 is true, so the ternary operator returns "Yes".

questions.question: Which statement is used for multi-way branching?
questions.explanation: switch is used when there are multiple possible branches based on a single expression.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for an if statement?
questions.explanation: The condition must be enclosed in parentheses, followed by braces for the block.

questions.question: What is the purpose of break in a switch statement?
options: To continue to the next case
questions.explanation: break is used to terminate the switch block and prevent fall-through to the next case.

questions.question: Which loop is guaranteed to execute at least once?
questions.explanation: do-while checks the condition after executing the loop body, so it runs at least once.

questions.question: Which loop checks the condition before executing the body?
questions.explanation: Both for and while loops check the condition before each iteration.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax of a for loop?
questions.explanation: The for loop uses semicolons to separate initialization, condition, and update.

questions.question: How many times does the loop for(int i=0;i<5;i++) execute?
questions.explanation: It runs for i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — a total of 5 times.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to exit a loop immediately?
questions.explanation: break terminates the loop immediately and transfers control to the statement after the loop.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to skip the current iteration and continue with the next?
questions.explanation: continue skips the remaining statements in the current iteration and proceeds to the next iteration.

questions.question: Which keyword is used for an unconditional jump in C++?
questions.explanation: goto transfers control unconditionally to a labeled statement.

questions.question: What is a class in C++?
options: A user-defined data type that binds data and functions together
questions.explanation: A class is a user-defined data type that encapsulates data members and member functions.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to define a class in C++?
questions.explanation: The class keyword is used to define a class in C++.

questions.question: By default, members of a class are:
questions.explanation: In a class, members are private by default.

questions.question: What is an object in C++?
questions.explanation: An object is a runtime instance of a class.

questions.question: What is class specification?
options: The declaration of a class including its data members and member functions
questions.explanation: Class specification declares the class, its data members, and member functions.

questions.question: What is the correct way to create an object of class Student?
questions.explanation: Objects are created using the syntax: ClassName objectName;

questions.question: How do you access a member of an object?
questions.explanation: The dot (.) operator is used to access members of an object.

questions.question: How do you access members through a pointer to an object?
questions.explanation: The arrow (->) operator is used to access members through a pointer to an object.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a constructor?
options: To initialize objects of a class
questions.explanation: A constructor is automatically called when an object is created to initialize it.

questions.question: What is the name of a constructor?
questions.explanation: A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type.

questions.question: Does a constructor have a return type?
options: No, it has no return type
questions.explanation: Constructors do not have a return type, not even void.

questions.question: What is a default constructor?
options: A constructor that takes two arguments
A constructor that takes one argument
A constructor that takes no arguments
questions.explanation: A default constructor takes no parameters and is called when no arguments are provided.

questions.question: What is a parameterized constructor?
options: A constructor that takes arguments to initialize the object
questions.explanation: A parameterized constructor accepts arguments to initialize data members with specific values.

questions.question: What is a copy constructor?
options: A constructor that deletes an object
A constructor that creates a new object as a copy of an existing object
questions.explanation: A copy constructor initializes a new object using an existing object of the same class.

questions.question: What is the parameter of a copy constructor?
options: A reference to an object of the same class
questions.explanation: A copy constructor takes a reference to an object of the same class, e.g., Student(const Student &s).

questions.question: Can constructors be overloaded?
questions.explanation: Constructors can be overloaded based on the number or type of parameters.

questions.question: When is a constructor called?
options: Automatically when an object is created
questions.explanation: A constructor is automatically invoked at the time of object creation.

questions.question: Can a constructor be called explicitly?
options: Yes, but only as a member function call
questions.explanation: A constructor can be called explicitly, but it creates a temporary object; it cannot be called like a normal function.

questions.question: What happens if no constructor is defined in a class?
options: The compiler provides a default constructor
questions.explanation: If no constructor is defined, the compiler generates a default constructor automatically.

questions.question: What is a destructor?
options: A special member function that is called when an object goes out of scope
questions.explanation: A destructor is called automatically when an object is destroyed.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax of a destructor for class MyClass?
questions.explanation: A destructor is declared with a tilde (~) before the class name.

questions.question: Can a destructor take arguments?
questions.explanation: A destructor cannot take arguments and cannot be overloaded.

questions.question: How many destructors can a class have?
questions.explanation: A class can have only one destructor.

questions.question: What is the main use of 'this' pointer?
options: It points to the base class
It points to the global variable
It points to the current object
questions.explanation: The this pointer holds the address of the object that invokes a member function.

questions.question: What is the type of 'this' pointer?
questions.explanation: The this pointer is of type ClassName* const inside non-const member functions.

questions.question: Can objects be passed as function arguments?
options: Yes, by value or by reference
questions.explanation: Objects can be passed to functions either by value (copy) or by reference.

questions.question: What is the difference between passing an object by value and by reference?
options: By value passes the original; by reference makes a copy
By value makes a copy; by reference passes the original object
questions.explanation: Passing by value copies the object; passing by reference passes the actual object.

questions.question: What is the advantage of passing objects by reference?
questions.explanation: Passing by reference avoids the overhead of copying large objects.

questions.question: How do you pass an object by reference to a function?
questions.explanation: A reference parameter is declared using & after the type, e.g., ClassName &obj.

questions.question: Can a function return an object?
options: Yes, by value or by reference
questions.explanation: A function can return an object either by value (a copy) or by reference.

questions.question: What happens when a function returns an object by value?
options: A copy of the object is returned
questions.explanation: Returning by value creates a copy of the object to be returned.

questions.question: What is a temporary object?
options: An unnamed object created by the compiler
questions.explanation: A temporary object is an unnamed object created by the compiler during expression evaluation.

questions.question: What is the scope of a class member?
questions.explanation: Class members are accessible throughout the class, subject to access specifiers.

questions.question: What is the use of access specifiers in a class?
options: To control the accessibility of class members
questions.explanation: Access specifiers (public, private, protected) control how class members can be accessed.

questions.question: Which access specifier allows members to be accessed from outside the class?
questions.explanation: Public members are accessible from anywhere in the program.

questions.question: Which access specifier restricts members to be accessed only within the class?
questions.explanation: Private members can only be accessed within the class.

questions.question: What is a member function?
options: A function defined inside a class
questions.explanation: A member function is a function that is declared inside a class and operates on its objects.

questions.question: How do you define a member function outside the class?
questions.explanation: The scope resolution operator (::) is used to define a member function outside the class.

questions.question: What is the default access specifier for members of a struct?
questions.explanation: In a struct, members are public by default.

questions.question: In C++20, which feature allows compile-time string manipulation?
questions.explanation: consteval forces a function to always produce a compile-time result, enabling compile-time string manipulation.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of std::sort on average?
questions.explanation: std::sort uses Introsort which has O(n log n) average and worst-case complexity.

questions.question: Which smart pointer owns a uniquely owned resource in C++?
questions.explanation: std::unique_ptr provides exclusive ownership of a dynamically allocated object.

questions.question: What does RAII stand for in C++?
questions.explanation: RAII binds resource lifetime to object lifetime — acquisition in constructor, release in destructor.

questions.question: In C++11, what does noexcept indicate?
options: The function may throw but is optimized
questions.explanation: noexcept specifies that a function will not throw exceptions; if it does, std::terminate is called.

questions.question: Which virtual function feature enables runtime polymorphism in C++?
questions.explanation: The vtable (virtual table) holds function pointers for dynamic dispatch of virtual functions.

questions.question: What is inheritance in C++?
options: The process of creating multiple objects
The process of deleting a class
The process of copying a function
The process by which one class acquires the properties and behaviors of another class
questions.explanation: Inheritance allows a new class (derived) to acquire properties and methods of an existing class (base).

questions.question: Which class is also known as the parent class?
questions.explanation: The base class is also called the parent or super class.

questions.question: Which class is also known as the child class?
questions.explanation: The derived class is also called the child or subclass.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for inheriting class Derived from class Base?
questions.explanation: The syntax is: class Derived : access_specifier Base { };

questions.question: What is the default access specifier for inheritance in a class?
questions.explanation: When inheriting with the class keyword, the default access specifier is private.

questions.question: What is the default access specifier for inheritance in a struct?
questions.explanation: When inheriting with the struct keyword, the default access specifier is public.

questions.question: In public inheritance, public members of the base class become:
questions.explanation: Public inheritance preserves the access levels of public members.

questions.question: In public inheritance, protected members of the base class become:
questions.explanation: Protected members remain protected in the derived class under public inheritance.

questions.question: In public inheritance, private members of the base class become:
questions.explanation: Private members of the base class are never directly accessible in the derived class.

questions.question: In private inheritance, public members of the base class become:
questions.explanation: Private inheritance makes all public and protected members private in the derived class.

questions.question: In protected inheritance, public members of the base class become:
questions.explanation: Protected inheritance makes public and protected members protected in the derived class.

questions.question: Which members of the base class are NOT accessible in the derived class?
questions.explanation: Private members of the base class are not directly accessible in the derived class.

questions.question: Which inheritance type creates an 'is-a' relationship?
questions.explanation: Public inheritance represents an 'is-a' relationship, e.g., a Car is a Vehicle.

questions.question: Which inheritance type creates a 'has-a' relationship?
questions.explanation: Private inheritance represents a 'has-a' or 'implemented-in-terms-of' relationship.

questions.question: When is the base class constructor called in inheritance?
options: Along with the derived class constructor
questions.explanation: Base class constructors are called before derived class constructors.

questions.question: When is the base class destructor called in inheritance?
options: Along with the derived class destructor
questions.explanation: Base class destructors are called after derived class destructors.

questions.question: How do you call a parameterized base class constructor from a derived class?
options: Inside the derived class constructor body
In the derived class constructor's initializer list
questions.explanation: Base class constructors with parameters are called using the initializer list, e.g., Derived() : Base(args).

questions.question: If a derived class constructor does not explicitly call a base class constructor, which one is called?
options: The default constructor of the base class
questions.explanation: If not specified, the compiler calls the default constructor of the base class.

questions.question: What is function overriding?
options: Defining multiple functions with the same name
Redefining a base class function in the derived class with the same signature
questions.explanation: Function overriding occurs when a derived class provides a new implementation for a base class function.

questions.question: What is the main difference between function overloading and function overriding?
options: Overloading is runtime, overriding is compile-time
Overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime
questions.explanation: Overloading is resolved at compile time, while overriding is resolved at runtime using virtual functions.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to enable runtime polymorphism in function overriding?
questions.explanation: The virtual keyword in the base class enables runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What is a class hierarchy?
options: A tree-like structure of classes related by inheritance
questions.explanation: A class hierarchy organizes classes in a tree structure based on inheritance.

questions.question: What is single inheritance?
options: A derived class inheriting from multiple base classes
A base class inheriting from derived class
A derived class inheriting from one base class
questions.explanation: Single inheritance means a derived class has only one base class.

questions.question: What is multiple inheritance?
options: A derived class inheriting from one base class
A derived class inheriting from multiple base classes
A base class inheriting from derived class
questions.explanation: Multiple inheritance allows a derived class to inherit from more than one base class.

questions.question: What is multilevel inheritance?
options: A base class inheriting from derived class
A derived class inheriting from multiple base classes
A derived class inheriting from another derived class
questions.explanation: Multilevel inheritance forms a chain, e.g., A → B → C.

questions.question: What is hierarchical inheritance?
options: A derived class inheriting from multiple base classes
A derived class inheriting from another derived class
Multiple derived classes inheriting from a single base class
questions.explanation: In hierarchical inheritance, one base class is inherited by multiple derived classes.

questions.question: What is hybrid inheritance?
options: A combination of two or more types of inheritance
questions.explanation: Hybrid inheritance combines multiple and multilevel inheritance.

questions.question: What is the diamond problem in multiple inheritance?
options: A syntax error in class definition
Ambiguity when a class inherits from two classes that share a common base class
questions.explanation: The diamond problem occurs when a derived class inherits from two classes with a common base, causing ambiguity.

questions.question: How is the diamond problem resolved in C++?
questions.explanation: Virtual inheritance ensures only one copy of the common base class is inherited.

questions.question: Which keyword is used for virtual inheritance?
questions.explanation: Virtual inheritance is declared as class Derived : virtual public Base.

questions.question: Which access specifier makes base class members accessible to derived class but not to outside code?
questions.explanation: Protected members are accessible in derived classes but not from outside.

questions.question: Can a derived class access private members of the base class directly?
questions.explanation: Private members of the base class cannot be accessed directly by the derived class.

questions.question: How can a derived class access private members of the base class?
options: By using the scope resolution operator
Through public or protected member functions of the base class
questions.explanation: The derived class can access private members through public or protected methods of the base class.

questions.question: What happens if a derived class defines a function with the same name as a base class function but different parameters?
options: The base class function is overridden
The base class function is hidden
questions.explanation: The base class function is hidden by the derived class function, not overridden.

questions.question: How do you call a hidden base class function from a derived class?
questions.explanation: Use the scope resolution operator: Base::functionName().

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT inherited by a derived class?
questions.explanation: Constructors and destructors are not inherited in C++.

questions.question: Can a derived class have additional members not present in the base class?
questions.explanation: A derived class can add its own data members and member functions.

questions.question: What is the size of a derived class object?
options: Exactly the size of the base class
Exactly the size of the derived class
At least the size of the base class plus derived class members
questions.explanation: A derived object includes base class members plus its own members.

questions.question: Can a base class pointer point to a derived class object?
questions.explanation: A base class pointer can point to a derived class object, which is called upcasting.

questions.question: Can a derived class pointer point to a base class object without explicit casting?
questions.explanation: Downcasting (base to derived) requires explicit casting.

questions.question: What is the main concept of OOP?
options: Binding data and functions into a single unit (object)
questions.explanation: OOP binds data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit called an object.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of OOP?
questions.explanation: OOP does not rely only on top-down execution. Its main characteristics are Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of OOP over procedural programming?
questions.explanation: OOP provides better data hiding (security) and code reuse through inheritance.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a class and an object?
options: Object is a blueprint, class is an instance
Class is a blueprint, object is an instance
questions.explanation: A class is a blueprint or template, and an object is a specific instance created from that class.

questions.question: Which OOP feature increases code reusability?
questions.explanation: Inheritance allows a new class to reuse the properties and methods of an existing class.

questions.question: What does encapsulation mean?
options: Binding data and functions into a single unit
questions.explanation: Encapsulation wraps data and the functions that manipulate it into a single unit (class).

questions.question: What is the main purpose of abstraction?
options: Hiding implementation details and showing only essential features
questions.explanation: Abstraction shows only essential features to the user while hiding internal implementation.

questions.question: What does polymorphism mean?
questions.explanation: Polymorphism means 'one name, many forms' — for example, function overloading and virtual functions.

questions.question: Who is the creator of C++?
questions.explanation: Bjarne Stroustrup created C++ at Bell Labs in 1979 as an extension of C with object-oriented features.

questions.question: What is the relationship between C and C++?
options: C is a superset of C++
C++ is a superset of C
questions.explanation: C++ is a superset of C — it includes all C features and adds object-oriented features.

questions.question: Why was OOP needed?
options: To overcome limitations of procedural programming
questions.explanation: OOP was introduced to solve problems like data insecurity, poor reusability, and difficulty in managing large programs in procedural programming.

questions.question: In procedural programming, what is the main focus?
questions.explanation: Procedural programming focuses on functions and step-by-step procedures, while OOP focuses on objects.

questions.question: What is a project-oriented approach in OOP?
options: Building software as a collection of interacting objects
questions.explanation: A project-oriented approach means designing software as a set of objects that interact with each other, making it modular and maintainable.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of reusability in OOP?
questions.explanation: Reusability allows existing code to be used again, reducing development time and effort.

questions.question: Encapsulation helps in:
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides internal data from outside interference, which is known as data hiding.

questions.question: Which access specifier makes class members accessible only within the class?
questions.explanation: Private members are accessible only within the class, which is a key part of encapsulation.

questions.question: What is inheritance in OOP?
options: Deriving a new class from an existing class
questions.explanation: Inheritance allows a new class (derived) to acquire properties and methods of an existing class (base).

questions.question: What is the base class in inheritance?
options: The class that is inherited from
questions.explanation: The base class is the existing class from which other classes inherit features.

questions.question: What is the derived class in inheritance?
options: The class that inherits from another class
questions.explanation: The derived class is the new class that inherits properties and methods from the base class.

questions.question: Compile-time polymorphism is achieved by:
questions.explanation: Function overloading and operator overloading are examples of compile-time polymorphism.

questions.question: Runtime polymorphism is achieved by:
questions.explanation: Virtual functions enable runtime polymorphism, where the function call is resolved at runtime.

questions.question: What is function overloading?
options: Different function names with same parameters
Same function name with same parameters
Same function name with different parameters
questions.explanation: Function overloading allows multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists.

questions.question: What is operator overloading?
options: Giving new meaning to an existing operator for user-defined types
questions.explanation: Operator overloading allows existing operators to work with user-defined data types.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of OOP?
questions.explanation: OOP aims to reduce complexity, not increase it. It provides reusability, security, and easier maintenance.

questions.question: In OOP, data and functions are combined into:
questions.explanation: In OOP, data and functions are encapsulated into objects.

questions.question: Which language was C++ derived from?
questions.explanation: C++ was derived from the C language, adding object-oriented features.

questions.question: What is the original name of C++?
questions.explanation: C++ was originally called 'C with Classes' before being renamed to C++.

questions.question: What does the '++' in C++ signify?
questions.explanation: The '++' is the increment operator, symbolizing an enhanced version of C.

questions.question: Which of the following is a procedural programming language?
questions.explanation: C is a procedural programming language, while C++, Java, and Python support OOP.

questions.question: In OOP, what is an object?
questions.explanation: An object is a runtime instance of a class.

questions.question: What is a class in OOP?
questions.explanation: A class is a blueprint or template that defines the properties and behavior of objects.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of encapsulation?
options: A class with private data members and public methods
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is achieved by making data members private and providing public methods to access them.

questions.question: What is data hiding in OOP?
options: Restricting access to internal data of a class
questions.explanation: Data hiding restricts direct access to internal data, usually achieved using private access specifier.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of OOP?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is one of the main characteristics of OOP.

questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of procedural programming?
questions.explanation: Procedural programming has poor data security and limited code reusability compared to OOP.

questions.question: Which of the following supports multiple inheritance in C++?
questions.explanation: C++ supports multiple inheritance through classes, where a derived class can inherit from multiple base classes.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'class' keyword in C++?
questions.explanation: The 'class' keyword is used to define a class in C++.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about OOP?
options: It makes programs more modular and maintainable
It removes the need for functions
It only works with small programs
questions.explanation: OOP makes programs more modular, maintainable, and reusable.

questions.question: What is the main goal of OOP?
options: To model real-world entities as objects
questions.explanation: OOP aims to model real-world entities as objects, making software design more intuitive.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an OOP language?
questions.explanation: C is a procedural language, while C++, Java, and Python support OOP.

questions.question: What is operator overloading in C++?
options: Changing the precedence of an operator
Giving new meaning to an existing operator for user-defined types
questions.explanation: Operator overloading allows existing operators to work with user-defined data types.

questions.question: Which of the following operators cannot be overloaded in C++?
questions.explanation: The scope resolution operator :: cannot be overloaded.

questions.question: Can operator overloading change the precedence of an operator?
questions.explanation: Operator overloading cannot change the precedence or associativity of an operator.

questions.question: Can operator overloading change the number of operands an operator takes?
questions.explanation: The arity (number of operands) of an operator cannot be changed.

questions.question: How many operands does a unary operator take?
questions.explanation: A unary operator takes one operand, e.g., ++, --, -.

questions.question: How many operands does a binary operator take?
questions.explanation: A binary operator takes two operands, e.g., +, -, *, /.

questions.question: Which operator must be overloaded as a member function?
questions.explanation: The assignment operator = must be overloaded as a non-static member function.

questions.question: Which of the following operators cannot be overloaded as a friend function?
questions.explanation: Operators =, [], (), and -> must be overloaded as member functions, not as friend functions.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for overloading the + operator as a member function?
options: friend ClassName operator+(const ClassName&, const ClassName&);
questions.explanation: A member function version takes one explicit parameter (the right operand).

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for overloading the + operator as a friend function?
options: friend ClassName operator+(const ClassName&, const ClassName&);
questions.explanation: A friend function takes two parameters, one for each operand.

questions.question: What is the typical return type of a binary arithmetic operator like +?
questions.explanation: Binary arithmetic operators usually return a new object by value.

questions.question: Why is a binary arithmetic operator usually returned by value?
options: To allow chaining and avoid dangling references
questions.explanation: Returning by value creates a new object that can be used in further expressions without referring to a local temporary.

questions.question: What is a temporary object in C++?
options: An unnamed object created by the compiler
questions.explanation: A temporary object is an unnamed object created during expression evaluation.

questions.question: When is a temporary object typically created?
options: When returning by value or during type conversions
questions.explanation: Temporary objects are often created when functions return by value or when implicit conversions occur.

questions.question: What is the main issue when overloading the increment operator?
options: Prefix and postfix versions have the same name
It must be a friend function
questions.explanation: Both prefix and postfix increment use operator++, so a dummy parameter is used to distinguish them.

questions.question: How do you distinguish prefix and postfix increment in operator overloading?
options: Prefix takes an int, postfix takes no argument
Prefix takes no argument, postfix takes a dummy int
questions.explanation: Prefix: operator++(); Postfix: operator++(int).

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for overloading the prefix increment operator?
questions.explanation: Prefix increment is declared as ClassName& operator++();

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for overloading the postfix increment operator?
questions.explanation: Postfix increment is declared as ClassName operator++(int);

questions.question: What is the typical return type of the prefix increment operator?
questions.explanation: Prefix increment usually returns a reference to the incremented object.

questions.question: What is the typical return type of the postfix increment operator?
questions.explanation: Postfix increment usually returns a copy of the object before incrementing.

questions.question: What is data conversion in the context of operator overloading?
options: Converting a pointer to an integer
Converting an operator to a function
Converting a class to a struct
Converting one user-defined type to another or to a built-in type
questions.explanation: Data conversion allows objects of one type to be converted to another type.

questions.question: How do you define a conversion operator to convert a class object to int?
questions.explanation: A conversion operator is declared as operator type() { }.

questions.question: Can a conversion operator take arguments?
questions.explanation: A conversion operator takes no arguments and returns the target type.

questions.question: Which of the following is a pitfall of operator overloading?
options: It cannot be used with classes
It can make code confusing if misused
questions.explanation: Overusing or misusing operator overloading can lead to confusing and error-prone code.

questions.question: What is a major pitfall of overloading the && and || operators?
questions.explanation: Overloading && and || removes the short-circuit behavior, which can lead to unexpected side effects.

questions.question: What is a pitfall of overloading the comma operator?
options: It can lead to unexpected behavior
questions.explanation: Overloading the comma operator is rarely needed and can cause confusing behavior.

questions.question: What is a pitfall of overloading the -> operator?
options: It must return a pointer or an object that supports ->
It must be a friend function
questions.explanation: The -> operator must ultimately return a pointer or another object that overloads ->.

questions.question: What is a pitfall of overloading new and delete?
options: It changes the size of objects
questions.explanation: Overloading new and delete requires careful memory management and can introduce bugs.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of operator overloading?
options: It makes user-defined types behave like built-in types
It eliminates the need for functions
questions.explanation: Operator overloading allows user-defined types to be used with operators in a natural way.

questions.question: Can operator overloading create new operators?
options: Yes, any operator can be created
No, only existing operators can be overloaded
questions.explanation: C++ does not allow creating new operators; only existing ones can be overloaded.

questions.question: Which of the following operators can be overloaded?
questions.explanation: + can be overloaded; ::, .*, ., ?:, and sizeof cannot be overloaded.

questions.question: Which of the following operators cannot be overloaded?
questions.explanation: The pointer-to-member operator .* cannot be overloaded.

questions.question: What is the correct way to overload the unary minus operator as a member function?
questions.explanation: Unary minus as a member takes no arguments.

questions.question: What is the correct way to overload the binary minus operator as a member function?
questions.explanation: Binary minus as a member takes one explicit parameter.

questions.question: What is the correct way to overload the binary minus operator as a friend function?
options: friend ClassName operator-(const ClassName&, const ClassName&);
questions.explanation: Binary minus as a friend takes two parameters, one for each operand.

questions.question: Which operator is commonly overloaded to allow input from cin?
questions.explanation: The extraction operator >> is overloaded for input.

questions.question: Which operator is commonly overloaded to allow output to cout?
questions.explanation: The insertion operator << is overloaded for output.

questions.question: When overloading << for output, what should it return?
questions.explanation: It should return ostream& to allow chaining like cout << a << b.

questions.question: When overloading >> for input, what should it return?
questions.explanation: It should return istream& to allow chaining like cin >> a >> b.

questions.question: Which operator must be overloaded as a non-static member function?
questions.explanation: The subscript operator [] must be a non-static member function.

questions.question: What is polymorphism in C++?
questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows using a single interface for different data types.

questions.question: What does polymorphism mean in C++?
questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows the same name to be used for different purposes, i.e., one name, many forms.

questions.question: Which of the following is a type of polymorphism in C++?
questions.explanation: C++ supports both compile-time (static) and runtime (dynamic) polymorphism.

questions.question: Compile-time polymorphism is also known as:
questions.explanation: Compile-time polymorphism is also called static or early binding.

questions.question: Runtime polymorphism is also known as:
questions.explanation: Runtime polymorphism is also called dynamic polymorphism or late binding.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of compile-time polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Function overloading is resolved at compile time.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of runtime polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Virtual functions enable runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: Function overloading is resolved at:
questions.explanation: The compiler decides which overloaded function to call based on arguments.

questions.question: Virtual functions are resolved at:
questions.explanation: Virtual function calls are resolved at runtime using the vtable.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to declare a virtual function?
questions.explanation: The virtual keyword is used in the base class to enable runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What is function overriding?
options: Defining multiple functions with the same name
Redefining a base class function in the derived class with the same signature
questions.explanation: Function overriding provides a new implementation for a base class virtual function in the derived class.

questions.question: Which of the following is necessary for runtime polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Runtime polymorphism requires inheritance and virtual functions.

questions.question: What is a pure virtual function?
options: A virtual function with a definition
A virtual function with no definition, declared as = 0
questions.explanation: A pure virtual function is declared with = 0 and makes the class abstract.

questions.question: What is an abstract class?
options: A class with only static members
A class that contains at least one pure virtual function
A class that cannot be inherited
questions.explanation: An abstract class has at least one pure virtual function and cannot be instantiated.

questions.question: Can an abstract class be instantiated?
questions.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly.

questions.question: What is a virtual destructor?
options: A destructor that deletes virtual functions
A destructor declared with the virtual keyword
A destructor that is pure virtual
A destructor that cannot be overloaded
questions.explanation: A virtual destructor ensures that the correct destructor is called when deleting a derived object via a base pointer.

questions.question: Why is a virtual destructor needed?
options: To properly destroy derived class objects through base class pointers
questions.explanation: Without a virtual destructor, deleting a derived object via a base pointer may cause undefined behavior.
Due to virtual function, the derived class version is called, so output is Derived.

questions.question: What is the output if the virtual keyword is removed from the base class show()?
questions.explanation: Without virtual, the function call is resolved at compile time based on the pointer type, so Base is called.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of polymorphism?
questions.explanation: Sequential is not a type of polymorphism.

questions.question: Operator overloading is an example of:
questions.explanation: Operator overloading is resolved at compile time.

questions.question: Function overriding is an example of:
questions.explanation: Function overriding with virtual functions is runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What is the vtable in C++?
options: A table of virtual function pointers
questions.explanation: The vtable is used to resolve virtual function calls at runtime.

questions.question: Which of the following can be virtual?
questions.explanation: Only member functions can be virtual. Constructors cannot be virtual.

questions.question: Can a constructor be virtual?
questions.explanation: Constructors cannot be virtual because the object's type is not fully determined until construction is complete.

questions.question: Can a destructor be virtual?
questions.explanation: Destructors can and should be virtual in base classes with virtual functions.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about pure virtual functions?
options: They have no body and are declared with = 0
questions.explanation: Pure virtual functions have no implementation in the base class and are declared with = 0.

questions.question: What happens if a derived class does not override a pure virtual function?
options: The base class function is called
The derived class also becomes abstract
The derived class can be instantiated
questions.explanation: If a derived class does not implement all pure virtual functions, it remains abstract.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of polymorphism?
options: It allows code to be written generically and reused
It removes the need for inheritance
questions.explanation: Polymorphism allows writing generic code that can work with objects of different types.

questions.question: Which of the following demonstrates polymorphism?
options: A base class pointer pointing to derived class objects
questions.explanation: Using a base class pointer to call virtual functions on derived objects is a classic example.
Without virtual, the function is called based on the pointer type, so A is printed.

questions.question: What is the output if show() is virtual in the above code?
questions.explanation: With virtual, the derived class version is called, so B is printed.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about virtual functions?
questions.explanation: Virtual functions are the mechanism for runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What is late binding?
options: Function call resolved at load time
Function call resolved at compile time
Function call resolved at link time
questions.explanation: Late binding means the function call is resolved at runtime, which is done via virtual functions.

questions.question: What is early binding?
options: Function call resolved at compile time
Function call resolved at link time
Function call resolved at load time
questions.explanation: Early binding means the function call is resolved at compile time, as in function overloading.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid use of polymorphism?
options: Using a base class pointer to call derived class methods
questions.explanation: Global variables are not related to polymorphism.

questions.question: Which of the following is a compile-time polymorphism technique?
questions.explanation: Templates are resolved at compile time, so they are compile-time polymorphism.
ptr points to a Derived object and print() is virtual, so Derived is printed.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about virtual functions and constructors?
options: Constructors cannot be virtual, but destructors can be
questions.explanation: Constructors cannot be virtual; destructors can and often should be virtual.

questions.question: What is the main difference between function overloading and function overriding?
options: Overloading is runtime, overriding is compile-time
Overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime
questions.explanation: Overloading is resolved at compile time; overriding is resolved at runtime with virtual functions.

questions.question: Which of the following allows a class to be polymorphic?
questions.explanation: Virtual functions make a class polymorphic by enabling runtime binding.

questions.question: Who is the creator of the C++ programming language?
questions.explanation: Bjarne Stroustrup created C++ at Bell Labs in 1979 as an extension of the C language with object-oriented features.

questions.question: Which operator is used to access members of a pointer to an object in C++?
questions.explanation: The -> (arrow) operator is used to access members of an object through a pointer, e.g., ptr->member.

questions.question: Which header file is required to use cout and cin in C++?
questions.explanation: <iostream> is the standard C++ header that provides cout, cin, cerr, and clog for input/output operations.

questions.question: What is the correct way to declare a reference to an integer in C++?
questions.explanation: int &ref = x; declares a reference ref that acts as an alias for the variable x. References must be initialized when declared.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to define a class in C++?
questions.explanation: The class keyword is used to define a class in C++. Its members are private by default, unlike struct where they are public.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'new' operator in C++?
options: Allocates memory dynamically on the heap
questions.explanation: The new operator dynamically allocates memory on the heap and returns a pointer to it. It replaces malloc() in C++.

questions.question: Which of the following is used for runtime polymorphism in C++?
questions.explanation: Virtual functions enable runtime polymorphism. They allow a derived class to override a base class method, resolved at runtime via vtable.

questions.question: What is the correct destructor syntax for a class named 'MyClass' in C++?
questions.explanation: A destructor is declared with a tilde (~) before the class name, e.g., ~MyClass(). It is called automatically when an object goes out of scope.

questions.question: Which concept allows the same function name to be used with different parameters in C++?
questions.explanation: Function overloading allows multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists, resolved at compile time.

questions.question: What does the '::' operator do in C++?
questions.explanation: The :: operator is the scope resolution operator. It is used to access global variables, class members, or namespace members, e.g., std::cout.

questions.question: What is a structure in C++?
options: A collection of variables of different data types under a single name
questions.explanation: A structure groups variables of different data types into a single unit.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to define a structure in C++?
questions.explanation: The struct keyword is used to define a structure.

questions.question: By default, members of a structure are:
questions.explanation: In C++, struct members are public by default.

questions.question: Can a structure in C++ contain functions?
questions.explanation: In C++, structures can have member functions, constructors, and destructors.

questions.question: How do you access members of a structure variable?
questions.explanation: The dot (.) operator is used to access members of a structure variable.

questions.question: How do you access members of a pointer to a structure?
questions.explanation: The arrow (->) operator is used to access members through a pointer to a structure.

questions.question: What is a nested structure?
options: A structure defined inside another structure
questions.explanation: A nested structure is a structure defined within another structure.

questions.question: How do you define a nested structure?
options: struct Outer { int x; } struct Inner;
struct Outer { struct Inner { int x; } in; };
questions.explanation: A structure can be defined inside another structure, and its variable can be declared as a member.

questions.question: What is an enumerated data type?
options: A user-defined data type with named integer constants
questions.explanation: enum is a user-defined data type that consists of named integer constants.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to define an enumeration?
questions.explanation: The enum keyword is used to define an enumeration.

questions.question: What is the default value of the first enumerator?
questions.explanation: By default, the first enumerator has value 0, and each subsequent one increments by 1.

questions.question: What is enum class in C++?
options: A scoped enumeration with type safety
questions.explanation: enum class provides scoped enumerations that are type-safe and do not implicitly convert to integers.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of enum class over plain enum?
questions.explanation: enum class prevents implicit conversions and keeps enumerators scoped within the enum name.

questions.question: What is a function prototype?
options: A declaration that tells the compiler about the function's name, return type, and parameters
questions.explanation: A function prototype declares the function before its use, specifying its signature.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for a function declaration?
questions.explanation: A function declaration includes the return type, name, and parameter list, ending with a semicolon.

questions.question: What is a function definition?
options: The actual implementation of the function with a body
questions.explanation: A function definition includes the function body with statements.

questions.question: What is the difference between call by value and call by reference?
options: Call by reference is not allowed in C++
Call by value passes the actual variable, call by reference passes a copy
Call by value passes a copy, call by reference passes the actual variable
questions.explanation: Call by value copies the argument, while call by reference passes the address (alias) of the argument.

questions.question: What is a reference argument?
options: A parameter that is an alias for the argument
questions.explanation: A reference parameter acts as an alias for the actual argument, allowing modification.

questions.question: How do you declare a reference parameter in C++?
questions.explanation: The & symbol after the type declares a reference parameter, e.g., int &x.

questions.question: What is function overloading?
options: Defining multiple functions with different names
Defining a function inside another function
Defining multiple functions with the same name but different parameters
questions.explanation: Function overloading allows multiple functions with the same name but different parameter lists.

questions.question: Can functions be overloaded based on return type only?
questions.explanation: Overloading requires a difference in the parameter list; return type alone is not sufficient.

questions.question: What is a default argument in a function?
options: An argument that is a reference
An argument that is always required
An argument that is a constant
An argument that has a default value if not provided
questions.explanation: Default arguments provide a value automatically if the caller omits that argument.

questions.question: Where are default arguments specified?
questions.explanation: Default arguments are specified in the function declaration, not in the definition or call.

questions.question: What is a storage class in C++?
options: It defines the size of a variable
It defines the data type of a variable
It defines the scope, lifetime, and visibility of a variable
It defines the value of a variable
questions.explanation: Storage classes specify the scope, lifetime, and linkage of variables and functions.

questions.question: Which storage class is the default for local variables?
questions.explanation: Local variables are auto by default, meaning they are created when the block is entered and destroyed when it exits.

questions.question: What is the lifetime of a static local variable?
questions.explanation: A static local variable retains its value between function calls and exists for the entire program.

questions.question: What does the extern storage class do?
options: Declares a variable that is defined in another file
questions.explanation: extern declares a variable or function that is defined in another translation unit.

questions.question: What is the register storage class used for?
options: To store the variable in hard disk
To suggest storing the variable in a CPU register for faster access
questions.explanation: register is a hint to the compiler to store the variable in a CPU register.

questions.question: What is the scope of a static global variable?
options: The function in which it is declared
The file in which it is declared
The block in which it is declared
questions.explanation: A static global variable is visible only within the file where it is declared.

questions.question: What is the difference between auto and register?
options: auto is for global, register is for local
auto is static, register is extern
auto is default, register is a hint for CPU register
questions.explanation: auto is the default storage for local variables, while register suggests faster access via CPU register.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the static keyword for a global variable?
options: To restrict its scope to the file
questions.explanation: A static global variable has internal linkage, meaning it can only be used within the same file.

questions.question: What is the return type of a function that returns nothing?
questions.explanation: void indicates that the function does not return a value.

questions.question: What is the correct way to pass an array to a function?
questions.explanation: Arrays are passed as pointers, so int arr[] or int *arr is used.

questions.question: What is the default access specifier for struct members?
questions.explanation: In a struct, members are public by default.

questions.question: What is the default access specifier for class members?
questions.explanation: In a class, members are private by default.

questions.question: How do you initialize a structure variable?
questions.explanation: Structure variables can be initialized using braces with values in order.

questions.question: What is an array of structures?
options: An array where each element is a structure
questions.explanation: An array of structures stores multiple structure variables in contiguous memory.

questions.question: Can a structure contain a pointer to itself?
options: Yes, for linked lists and trees
questions.explanation: A structure can contain a pointer to its own type, which is useful for self-referential data structures.

questions.question: What is the size of an empty structure in C++?
questions.explanation: An empty structure has a size of 1 byte in C++ to ensure unique addresses.

questions.question: What is the output of enum { RED, GREEN = 5, BLUE };?
questions.explanation: RED is 0 by default, GREEN is explicitly 5, and BLUE increments to 6.

questions.question: Which is the longest river in Asia?
questions.explanation: The Yangtze River at 6,300 km is the longest river in Asia and third-longest in the world.

questions.question: Which country has the largest population in Asia?
questions.explanation: China has the largest population in Asia with over 1.4 billion people.

questions.question: Mount Everest is located on the border of which countries?
questions.explanation: Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and China (Tibet Autonomous Region).

questions.question: The Dead Sea borders which countries?
questions.explanation: The Dead Sea borders Israel and Jordan, known for its extremely high salinity.

questions.question: Which is the smallest country in Southeast Asia by area?
questions.explanation: Singapore is the smallest country in Southeast Asia by land area at about 733 km².

questions.question: The Gobi Desert is located in which countries?
questions.explanation: The Gobi Desert spans northern China and southern Mongolia.

questions.question: In which year did the Battle of Plassey take place?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 and established British East India Company's rule.

questions.question: Who led the Quit India Movement of 1942?
questions.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement on 8 August 1942 with the 'Do or Die' slogan.

questions.question: The Chola dynasty was known for its mastery in which field?
questions.explanation: The Chola dynasty excelled in naval warfare and built magnificent temples like Brihadeeswara.

questions.question: In which year did India adopt its constitution?
questions.explanation: The Indian Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, making India a republic.

questions.question: Who was the first Governor-General of independent India?
questions.explanation: Lord Mountbatten served as the last Viceroy and first Governor-General of independent India.

questions.question: The Indus Valley Civilization was contemporary with which ancient civilization?
questions.explanation: The Indus Valley Civilization (c. 3300-1300 BCE) was contemporary with Mesopotamia and Egypt.

questions.question: What is the value of Euler's number e (approximately)?
questions.explanation: Euler's number e ≈ 2.71828 is the base of natural logarithms.

questions.question: Which theorem states that every integer greater than 1 is either prime or can be expressed as a product of primes?
questions.explanation: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees unique prime factorization for every integer > 1.

questions.question: What is the derivative of e^x?
questions.explanation: The exponential function is its own derivative: d/dx(e^x) = e^x.

questions.question: In group theory, what is an abelian group?
options: A group where operation is commutative
questions.explanation: An abelian group has a commutative operation: a·b = b·a for all elements a, b.

questions.question: What is the Riemann Hypothesis about?
questions.explanation: The Riemann Hypothesis concerns the distribution of zeros of the Riemann zeta function, deeply connected to prime numbers.

questions.question: What does Gödel's Incompleteness Theorem prove?
options: Any consistent formal system has true statements it cannot prove
questions.explanation: Gödel proved that in any consistent formal system, there exist true statements that cannot be proved within that system.

questions.question: What is the unit of quantum of energy?
questions.explanation: The electron-volt (eV) is the energy gained by one electron accelerating through 1 volt potential difference.

questions.question: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle states that ___ cannot both be known precisely.
questions.explanation: Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2 — position and momentum cannot both be precisely determined simultaneously.

questions.question: What is quantum entanglement?
options: Particles share the same quantum state
questions.explanation: Entanglement creates correlations between particles such that measuring one instantly determines the other's state.

questions.question: Schrödinger's equation describes the evolution of ___.
questions.explanation: The time-dependent Schrödinger equation governs how the quantum wave function evolves over time.

questions.question: Which principle explains electron orbital shapes?
questions.explanation: The Pauli exclusion principle prevents two electrons from occupying the same quantum state, defining orbital structure.

questions.question: What is a qubit?
questions.explanation: A qubit (quantum bit) is the fundamental unit of quantum information, existing in superposition of |0⟩ and |1⟩.

questions.question: Which country won the 2023 Cricket World Cup?
questions.explanation: Australia won the 2023 Cricket World Cup, beating India in the final at Ahmedabad.

questions.question: Who holds the record for the highest individual Test score?
questions.explanation: Matthew Hayden scored 380 against Zimbabwe in 2003, the highest individual Test score.

questions.question: How many overs are in a One Day International (ODI) match?
questions.explanation: An ODI match consists of 50 overs per side.

questions.question: Which bowler has taken the most Test wickets in cricket history?
questions.explanation: Muttiah Muralitharan holds the record with 800 Test wickets.

questions.question: What is the name of the cricket tournament played between England and Australia?
questions.explanation: The Ashes is a Test cricket series played between England and Australia since 1882.

questions.question: Which Indian cricketer scored a century in all international formats?
questions.explanation: Virat Kohli is the only Indian cricketer to score centuries in all three international formats.
